historical_record.description: Congregation Ohabai Shalom, formed in 1862, built its temple here in 1895 to a design by the architect Moses J. Lyon, in an eclectic style drawing on Moorish and Eastern European precedent. It is one of only three 19th-century synagogues left standing in California.

Bought in 1934 by the Soto Zen congregation as the synagogue's membership dwindled. The building housed the Japanese Zen community for more than forty years, and Shunryu Suzuki taught zazen here to students from outside the community in the 1960s and 1970s; the congregation withdrew in the 1970s to build new quarters nearby.

Offered for sale by the Redevelopment Agency in July 1975 as the Soto Zen Mission, at a minimum bid of $39,600, with priority given to holders of Residential Certificates of Preference — property owners who had lost buildings to eminent domain.

Designated a City of San Francisco landmark under Article 10 of the Planning Code as the Bush Street Temple, for its architecture and its history as a synagogue. It is the only designated property in the Japantown survey area with a recorded tie to Japanese American heritage.

unknowns: The city's Japantown context statement gives 1881 Bush Street for the temple Congregation Ohabai Shalom built in 1895 and 1831 Bush Street for the same congregation's synagogue on the evidence of the 1893 and 1899 Sanborn maps. It does not reconcile the two numbers.
